newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian Airlines plots flight out of the red.
newsitem.headline: Canadian Airlines plots flight out of the red.

text.p: Canadian Airlines Corp., newly armed with hard-won cost savings from unions, governments and 33 percent-owner AMR Corp., now faces a four-year overhaul to stem chronic financial losses.

The struggling Calgary-based carrier will focus on expanding its business to Asia through Vancouver, British Columbia, and wringing cost savings from its domestic routes by lowering capacity and filling smaller aircraft within Canada.

The moves, to be helped in the short term by postponing debt payments to bolster Canadian's precarious cash position, are part of a four-year strategy aimed at returning the airline to profitability for the first time since 1988.

"If they don't start showing the signs of that performance in the first six to 12 months, I don't think they'll get the whole four years to play it out," said Anthony Perl, a professor of transportation policy at the University of Calgary.

The company's restructuring plan, which includes employee wage cuts, government concessions, a reduction in fees paid to AMR, the parent of American Airlines, and major route changes, is aimed at adding C$800 million ($592 million) to its bottom line over four years.
The plan, which Canadian called essential to its survival, won the approval over the weekend of the Canadian Auto Workers (CAW), the last union to resist concessions.

Canadian hopes to boost its service by 20 percent in the growing Asian region, its most lucrative market. Under the scenario, Vancouver would become North America's biggest gateway to the Asia-Pacific region and a major hub for Fort Worth, Texas-based American Airlines.
Canadian, hoping to avert a cash crunch that was expected to hit early in 1997 without the restructuring plan, also plans to double its flight frequency to U.S. cities.

Perl said Canadian's plans to become a premier carrier to Asia depended on attracting a much larger number of passengers from U.S. and Asian centres because there were not enough business travelers in Canada to feed the strategy.
American Airlines, Canadian's code-sharing partner, was expected to play a key role in the strategy's success. Code sharing allows passengers to fly on both carriers with one ticket.
"To the extent that Americans use Canadian to get to Asia is entirely dependent on American Airlines and how it decides to structure its trans-Pacific services," Perl said.

Canadian also plans to cut its capacity within Canada, which has been cited as a major reason for its financial woes as it competed tooth and nail against major competitor Air Canada and upstart discount flyers.
One route singled out as a cash drain is the Toronto-Ottawa-Montreal triangle, where Canadian competes with Air Canada, the country's biggest carrier.

Canadian Chief Executive Kevin Benson was set to travel to Tokyo and London this week to continue meetings with the airline's 70 creditors, which are being asked to let Canadian postpone C$170 million ($126 million) of debt and aircraft lease payments until May.
Canadian Airlines shares closed up C18 cents (13 cents) to C$2.36 ($1.75) on the Toronto Stock Exchange on Monday, the first day of trading after the CAW agreed to support the survival plan.
